forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bolton to use £30m reserves over three years to bridge budget gap
news_drafts.lead: Bolton Council is planning to use £30m from its reserves over three years ending 2027 to bridge funding gaps, according to its medium-term financial strategy. The Audit Committee heard that external auditors have characterised the planned drawdown as "unsustainable reliance on reserves and a lack of action to address the underlying reasons for persistent overspending". Auditors identified that asset ceiling interest of £31.5m had not been included in the council's pension accounting, requiring a revised actuary report. They also raised control weaknesses across asset management and governance, including a failure to maintain the Corporate Risk Register during 2023–24. The council is receiving support from Manchester and Salford councils on internal audit delivery while developing a resource strategy to address staffing constraints.

news_drafts.headline: Bolton forecasts £10.5m overspend on schools grant for special needs in 2026-27, with a DfE plan pending
news_drafts.lead:
Bolton expects to spend £10.5m more than its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) in 2026-27, according to first-quarter monitoring papers for the council's Schools Forum. The whole of the overspend falls on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The council forecasts high needs spending of £72.409m against a net budget of £61.869m. Schools' delegated budgets, the money passed directly to individual schools, are on plan. Adding this year's overspend to deficits carried forward, the central reserve for the grant (money set aside, here in deficit) is projected at negative £29.745m at 31 March 2027.

Bolton has submitted a plan to reform special educational needs provision to the Department for Education. The department's decision on it will determine whether Bolton receives a High Needs Sustainability Grant to address the deficit. The papers show a potential grant of £10.539m, matching the forecast overspend. Neither approval nor an award has yet been confirmed.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: The paper gives the Bank of England base rate as 3.75% at 18 December 2025 and says financial markets are pricing a rise to around 4.0% by the end of 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the base rate peaked at 5.25% in August 2023 and fell to 3.75% by 18 December 2025. It says current market expectations suggest a modest increase during 2026, to around 4.0% by year end.
findings.matters: Expected base rate movement bears directly on the cost of replacement borrowing and the return on short-term deposits, which a finance director or lender would model.
findings.figures: Base rate 5.25% peak in August 2023; 3.75% at 18 December 2025; market expectation around 4.0% by end of 2026.
findings.quote: financial markets pricing in a rise to around 4.0% by the end of the year

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: All treasury and prudential indicators were within their approved limits at the end of quarter one 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper states that no indicator was exceeded, covering the authorised limit, operational boundary, interest rate exposures, maturity structure and the 364-day investment limit. The authorised limit and operational boundary are both shown at £281.5m, against debt of £148.0m.
findings.matters: A clean quarter-one record against the Budget Council limits is the evidence a finance director would use to show the approved treasury strategy is being operated as set.
findings.figures: Authorised limit £281.5m; debt £148.0m; fixed borrowing 100% against a 100% limit; investments 62% fixed and 38% variable against 100% and 50% limits.
findings.quote: As at the end of quarter one 2026/27 all indicators are within the limits approved at Budget Council.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: No investments were held beyond 364 days at quarter one, against a £15m limit, and the weighted average life of investments is approximately 35.13 weeks.
findings.detail: The paper reports £0m invested for more than 364 days against a maximum of £15m. It separately gives a weighted average life of approximately 35.13 weeks for the investments outstanding at 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: A zero balance beyond 364 days and a short average life show how much of the reserve cash is held for short-notice use, which a peer would compare with its own 364-day limit.
findings.figures: £0m invested beyond 364 days; £15m limit; weighted average life approximately 35.13 weeks.
findings.quote: The Weighted Average Life is approximately 35.13 weeks.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: £110.325m of short-term cash is placed in 15 deposits with 12 other councils and Horwich Town Council, at rates of 4.20% to 4.70%.
findings.detail: The paper lists short-term investments totalling £110,325,000 across 15 deposits, with rates from 4.20% (Blackpool Council) to 4.70% (Babergh District Council). Money market funds of £68,550,000 bring total investments to £178,875,000.
findings.matters: The rates and counterparties show the council lending its reserve cash to peers, which is the market a finance officer at another council would price against.
findings.figures: £110,325,000 short-term investments in 15 deposits; £68,550,000 money market funds; £178,875,000 total investments; rates 4.20% to 4.70%.
findings.quote: Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council Short Term 4.60 10,000,000

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: £118,000,000, or 79.73% of borrowing, falls due in 30 to 35 years, against an 80.00% upper limit in the maturity structure indicator.
findings.detail: The maturity table places £20,000,000 (13.51%) in 25 to 30 years, £118,000,000 (79.73%) in 30 to 35 years and £10,000,000 (6.76%) in 45 to 50 years. The paper says the upper and lower limits were not breached at any point in the year.
findings.matters: A large share of debt maturing in one band sits close to the prudential ceiling, which is the figure a peer council would compare when setting its own maturity profile and refinancing plan.
